Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\\n- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference paper and code repository. \\n- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \\n- We will assess your correctness on **matching the loading and processing described in the reference texts and code**. \\n\\n## Reference Information\\n\\n- The reference **paper** \\\"A flexible hippocampal population code for experience relative to reward\\\" is in the file `paper.pdf`.\\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `methods.txt`. \\n- **Code** from the paper are in the directory `code`.\\n- **Data** from the paper are in the directory `data`.\\n- **Documentation** on nwb file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io/en/latest/\\n\\n## Decoder Task\\n\\nTemporally align based on start of the trial. \\n\\n### Decoder Inputs:\\n- Time from start of trial in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\\n- Environment type (binary, ENV1 vs ENV2, per trial)\\n- Trial number (continuous, per trial)\\n- Previous trial outcome (binary, omitted = 0, rewarded = 1, per trial)\\n\\n### Decoder Outputs\\n- Distance to any location in the reward zone, time-varying. Discretization bins:\\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\\n  - 3: 0 cm\\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\\n  - 6: > +50 cm\\n- Absolute position in corridor, discretized into 5 equal-sized bins, time-varying\\n- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\\n  - 0: < 2 cm/s\\n  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\\n  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\\n  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\\n  - 4: > 40 cm/s\\n- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\\n- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\\n- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\\n\\n## Target Data Format\\n\\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\\n\\n```python\\ndata = {\\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. Discretization bins:\\n  - 0:  < -50 cm\\n  - 1: -50 to -10 cm\\n  - 2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\\n  - 3: 0 cm\\n  - 4: >0 cm to +10 cm\\n  - 5: +10 to +50 cm\\n  - 6: > +50 cm\\n- Absolute position in corridor, discretized into 5 equal-sized bins, time-varying\\n- Speed, time-varying. Discretized into bins:\\n  - 0: < 2 cm/s\\n  - 1: 2-10 cm/s\\n  - 2: 10-20 cm/s\\n  - 3: 20-40 cm/s\\n  - 4: > 40 cm/s\\n- Lick, time-varying. 0 = no, 1 = yes\\n- Reward zone location, per-trial. 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C\\n- Reward outcome, per-trial. 0 = no, 1 = yes\\n\\n## Target Data Format\\n\\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\\n\\n```python\\ndata = {\\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference paper and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference paper and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. Each step has explicit completion criteria. Do not proceed to the next step until the current step is complete. Do NOT look outside this project directory.\\n\\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Look for documentation or README files in the `code` directory\\n- Read the provided reference code bases to see how the reference paper loaded and manipulated the data\\n- Understand which functions are being called to read, curate, process, and manipulate the data\\n- For neural imaging data, does delta F over F need to be computed? \\n- For electrophysiology neural data, do cells need to be filtered based on quality? \\n- Note to file important functions, their inputs, and outputs\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented key functions and their purposes in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 1\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 2, update Step 1 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 2: Dataset Exploration\\n\\n**⚠️ CONSTRAINT REMINDER**: Only look at data in the `data` directory. Any information about dataset size (number of neurons, subjects, sessions, trials)\\n  - Fraction of data with different values, e.g. fraction of rewarded outcomes\\n  - Data processing, curation, and filtering\\n  - Variables important to experiments\\n  - Temporal alignment\\n  - Temporal binning\\n- Read the reference paper to find information about expected decoder accuracy.\\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented expected dataset statistics and processing details in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 3\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 4, update Step 3 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 4: Check for Consistency\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify your understanding is consistent across all sources. \\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Compare your understanding of:\\n  - Important functions from exploring the reference code\\n  - Dataset structure from exploring the dataset\\n  - Analysis described in the reference texts\\n- Note and investigate any discrepancies\\n- In particular, look for discrepancies in:\\n  - Experimental and behavioral variables\\n  - Data processing\\n  - Data curation\\n- Iterate until your understanding of the reference code, dataset, and reference texts are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**: You have resolved all discrepancies and documented your final understanding in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 4\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ CHECKPOINT**: Before proceeding to Step 5, update Step 4 CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 5: Mapping Planning\\n\\n**Goal**: Create a detailed plan for mapping source data to target format.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Map source data elements to target format components:\\n  - Run `python -u convert_data.py sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee conversion_sample_out.txt`\\n  a. Verify the sample data structure matches the specification.\\n  b. Check dimensions are consistent across trials/sessions.\\n  c. Check that no data is missed during conversion. \\n  d. Validate that metadata accurately describes the data.\\n2. When you do this, make sure that your estimate accounts for differences in lengths/numbers of trials/sessions. \\n  c. If full conversion time estimate is longer than 15 minutes, speed up the code by writing more efficient code (vectorizing loops, removing unnecessary or redundant computations) and/or including parallel processing. \\n3. Verify no errors reported.\\n  b. Attempt to address any warnings\\n  c. Check input ranges and output value distributions against expectations from reference texts.\\n\\n**Done when**: \\n- `sample_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `verification_sample_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- Processing plots show no anomalies\\n- Document sample statistics in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 7\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 8 until `sample_data.pkl` and `verification_sample_out.txt` files exist, and CONVERSION_NOTES.md Step 7 is filled in. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 8: Sample Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Verify the decoder runs successfully on sample data.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u convert_data.py converted_data.pkl --full 2>&1 | tee conversion_full_out.txt`\\n4. As the code runs, update your estimates of how long processing will take. If it is much longer than your previous estimate (> 1.5x), kill the process, optimize bottlenecks, and repeat. \\n5. Spot-check a few sessions to verify data integrity\\n8. **Check for consistency** between dataset statistics in `verification_full_out.txt` and the reference texts\\n9. Investigate any inconsistencies, and revise the conversion script until all dataset statistics are consistent\\n\\n**Done when**:\\n- `converted_data.pkl` is created and passes manual inspection\\n- `verification_full_out.txt` is created and passes inspection\\n- **ALL** dataset statistics are consistent with values from reference texts\\n- You have documented statistics and consistency in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 9\\\"\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 10 until `converted_data.pkl` and `verification_full_out.txt` files exist and CONVERSION_NOTES.MD Step 9 is filled in.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 10: Critical Review 1\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain.\\n\\n**Check 1: Output log verification**\\nRead through `verification_full_out.txt` to find and fix **all errors**. Explain why each warning could not be fixed in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 2: Construct sanity checks**\\n- Develop at least one sanity check each on neural, input, and output data.\\n- These must involve loading in the original data files (NOT through your conversion code).\\n- Construct comparison tests and criteria using `np.allclose()`. \\n- These tests can be spot-checks of the data, e.g. neural activity at trial 5, timepoint 10, neuron 3. \\n- Fix all mismatches/sanity check failures. \\n- Document your sanity checks to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 3: Reference code comparison**\\n- Compare your code to the reference code and methods. \\n- For each major processing step — (a) data loading, (b) neuron/trial filtering, (c) temporal alignment, (d) binning, (e) input construction, (f) output construction — identify the corresponding code in your script and in the reference, and compare the logic. \\n- Check whether you use the same variables, filtering, and processing as the reference code. \\n- Fix any mismatches. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n- Explain your reasoning for any differences in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`.\\n\\n**Check 4: Key statistics comparison**\\n- Verify that key statistics (number of animals, sessions, trials, neurons, input and output ranges, output distributions) match information available in the reference paper. \\n- Write code to investigate any discrepancies. \\n- Fix any discovered issues. \\n- Document your comparisons in `CONVERSION_NOTES.md`. \\n\\n**Check 5: Check for edge cases**\\n- Check for off-by-one errors at the beginning/ends of trials, sessions, and subjects, or in definitions of the inputs and outputs. \\n- There may be minor issues in the data that your code must handle. Check that your code robustly handles issues in the original data. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\nWrite a report to CONVERSION_NOTES.md describing **every** check you did, to help convince the user that the conversion code works. **Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 10\\\".\\n\\n**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 11 until you have checked for consistency between **every** statistic in the reference texts, code, and data and documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under Step 10. \\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 11: Full Decoder Training\\n\\n**Goal**: Validate the decoder on the **complete** dataset.\\n\\n**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: This step must complete fully. Do not skip or abbreviate. Do not proceed to Step 12 until this step is completely finished.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n1. Run `python -u train_decoder.py converted_data.pkl --plot-samples 2>&1 | tee train_decoder_full_out.txt`. If the GPU does not have sufficient RAM for the network training, use the flag `--cpu` to specify to use the CPU to train. \\n2. **Wait for complete execution** — this may take significant time for large datasets\\n3. **Check training**: Verify loss decreases over epochs\\n4. **Check accuracy**: High accuracy is an indicator that data conversion has been done correctly. Accuracy near chance is a sign that there might be issues in temporal alignment of signals, choice of data streams, or filtering or processing of data. Compare accuracy to expectations based on the paper. \\n\\n**Done when**: \\n1. Full decoder training completes (the script finishes running)\\n2. Accuracy results are documented in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 11\\\" with a table of accuracies\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 12: Critical Review 2\\n\\n**Goal**: Find and fix any errors by performing the following checks. Fix issues and re-run affected steps. Iterate until no issues remain. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to paper**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference paper\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the paper's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and paper. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `cache/` folder\\n- Create `cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \\n   303→\\n   304→ii. I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \\n   339→\\n   340→## 7-b. The value is constant across all timepoints within a trial.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\nif trial == 0:\\n    input_curr[3,:] = 0\\nelse:\\n    prev_reward_idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial-1], trial_end_idx[trial-1], dtype=int)\\n    isprevreward = np.any(isreward[prev_reward_idx])\\n    input_curr[3,:] = int(isprevreward)\\n```\\n\\niii. The instructions specify previous trial outcome as binary (omitted=0, rewarded=1). The code checks if any reward event fell within the previous trial's time boundaries.\\n\\n## 7-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Distance to reward zone* derived from?\\n\\ni. Derived from the `position` behavior time series and the reward zone location for the current trial. The reward zone boundaries come from the `reward_zone` behavior time series. This variable is non-zero when the mouse is in the reward zone. I combine this with the position of the mouse when this is non-zero to figure out the closest reward zone. To allow for some noise (of unknown source) and unrewarded tasks, I use the Viterbi algorithm to assign zones so that the rewarded positions match the known reward zones and it is uncommon to switch reward zone. \\n\\nii. Assigning reward zone location for each trial: \\n- Before converting, the `survey()` function was used to try to understand all the data values, including whatever is going on with the `reward_zone` variable. It first computes the position of the min and max position of the mouse when `reward_zone` is non-zero:\\n```python\\nbehavior_data = nwbfile.processing['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series       \\ninfo['reward_zone_positions'] = np.full((ntrials, 2), np.nan)\\nposition = behavior_data['position'].data[:]\\nfor trial in range(ntrials):\\n    idx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\\n    pos_trial = position[idx]\\n    reward_zone_trial = reward_zone[idx] > 0\\n    if not np.any(reward_zone_trial):\\n        continue\\n    info['reward_zone_positions'][trial] = [np.min(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial]), np.max(pos_trial[reward_zone_trial])]\\n```\\nThe function `segment_reward_positions()` uses the Viterbi algorithm to assign reward zone labels so that the initial rewarded positions are close to the corresponding rewarded zone:\\n```python\\nreward_zone_dict = {'A': [80, 130],\\n                    'B': [200, 250],\\n                    'C': [320, 370]}\\n...\\nsigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\\nzone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\\ndist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\\n                    startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\\ndist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\\nlog_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\\n```\\nIt also encourages the reward zone label to not change often:\\n```python\\npstay = .9\\nlog_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\\nnp.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\\n```\\n\\niii. The paper defines reward zones A, B, C at specific position ranges. These same ranges could also be found, with some translation, in the code (required mapping X -> A, etc.). I plotted the position of the mouse when `reward_zone` was positive (note that the value was between 0 and 6 I think) to determine that the Viterbi approach would likely work, and that the start of the rewarded position was the least noisy variable to use. The class fractions were approximately 1/3 after this, so it seemed correct. \\n\\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Distance to reward zone*?\\n\\ni. For each timepoint, compute the signed distance from the animal's position to the nearest edge of the reward zone. Distance is 0 when inside the zone, negative when before the zone, and positive when past it.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\ndef compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position_curr, reward_zone_curr):\\n    ntimepoints = len(position_curr)\\n    reward_zone_range = reward_zone_dict[reward_zone_curr]\\n    distance_to_reward_zone = np.zeros(ntimepoints)\\n    idx_before_zone = position_curr < reward_zone_range[0]\\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_before_zone] = position_curr[idx_before_zone] - reward_zone_range[0]\\n    idx_after_zone = position_curr > reward_zone_range[1]\\n    distance_to_reward_zone[idx_after_zone] = position_curr[idx_after_zone] - reward_zone_range[1]\\n    return distance_to_reward_zone\\n```\\n\\niii. This matches the paper's concept of distance relative to the reward zone. The reward zone boundaries are from `reward_zone_dict`, inspired by the reference code `Sosa_et_al_2024/src/reward_relative/behavior.py`.\\n\\n## 7-c. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* thresholded into categories?\\n\\ni. The continuous distance is discretized into 7 bins using `np.digitize` with bin edges `[-inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, inf]`.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\ndistance_to_reward_zone_bins = [-np.inf, -50, -10, 0, 1e-6, 10, 50, np.inf]\\n...\\noutput_curr[0] = np.digitize(distance_to_reward_zone, distance_to_reward_zone_bins) - 1\\n```\\n\\niii. The bin edges match the instructions. The `1e-6` boundary separates exactly 0 (in the zone boundary) from slightly positive. The `-1` corrects `np.digitize` to be 0-indexed.\\n\\n## 7-d. How is `output` *Distance to reward zone* aligned with the neural data?\\n\\ni. The position data and neural data share the same time indices within each trial, so no additional alignment is needed.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\nidx = np.arange(trial_start_idx[trial], trial_end_idx[trial], dtype=int)\\nspike_data_curr = spike_data[idx]\\nposition_curr = position[idx]\\n```\\n\\niii. Both neural and behavioral data use the same time indexing (verified by timestamp assertions earlier in the code), so indexing by the same `idx` array ensures alignment.\\n\\n## 8-a. No processing beyond extracting the per-trial slice and discretizing.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\nposition_curr = position[idx]\\noutput_curr[1] = np.digitize(position_curr, position_bins) - 1\\n```\\n\\niii. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\\n\\ni. Several cases are handled:\\n- **Neural/behavior length mismatch**: If the number of neural time bins differs from behavior timestamps, data is cropped to the minimum of the two with a warning printed.\\n- **Short trials**: Trials with fewer than 50 timepoints (`min_ntimepoints`) are skipped with a warning.\\n- **Missing reward zone data**: Trials where `reward_zone` is never active (all zeros) get NaN positions, and the Viterbi algorithm handles these via uniform emission (assignment driven by neighboring trials' transitions).\\n- **Reward timestamp alignment**: An assertion verifies reward times align within half a time bin of behavior timestamps.\\n\\nii.\\n```python\\nif T != len(timestamps):\\n    print(f\\\"Warning: number of neural time bins ({T}) does not match number of behavior timestamps ({len(timestamps)}), cropping to the minimum of the two\\\")\\n    T = min(T, len(timestamps))\\n    spike_data = spike_data[:T]\\n    timestamps = timestamps[:T]\\n...\\nif idx.sum() < min_ntimepoints:\\n    print(f\\\"Skipping trial {trial}...\\\")\\n    istrial[trial] = False\\n    continue\\n```\\n\\niii. These are defensive checks found during data exploration. The neural/behavior mismatch occurs in a small number of sessions.\\n\\n## 13-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\\n\\ni.  399→    all_info = {}\\n   400→    subjects = get_subjects(datadir=datadir)\\n   401→    all_info['reward_zone_positions'] = {}\\n   402→    fig,ax = plt.subplots(1,len(subjects),   464→    with open(surveyfile, 'wb') as f:\\n   465→        pickle.dump(all_info, f)\\n   466→        \\n   467→    return all_info\\n   468→\\n   469→def segment_reward_positions(reward_zone_positions):\\n   470→    # assign each trial to one of the reward zones defined in reward_zone_dict\\n   471→    # use viterbi algorithm with a high cost for switching to encourage stable assignments\\n   472→    zone_names = sorted(reward_zone_dict.keys())\\n   473→    n_states = len(zone_names)\\n   474→    zone_ranges = np.array([reward_zone_dict[z] for z in zone_names])  # (n_states, 2)\\n   475→    pstay = .9\\n   476→    sigma = 10.0  # std dev for Gaussian emission on zone distance\\n   477→\\n   478→    # transition log-probabilities\\n   479→    log_trans = np.full((n_states, n_states), np.log((1 - pstay) / (n_states - 1)))\\n   480→    np.fill_diagonal(log_trans, np.log(pstay))\\n   481→\\n   482→    results = {}\\n   483→\\n   484→    for mouse_id, positions in reward_zone_positions.items():\\n   485→        n_trials = positions.shape[0]\\n   486→        startpoints = positions[:,0] # use the start point as it looks cleaner\\n   487→        valid = ~np.isnan(startpoints)\\n   488→\\n   489→        # emission log-probabilities: Gaussian penalty based on distance to zone range\\n   490→        # distance is 0 if inside [lo, hi], otherwise distance to nearest edge\\n   491→        # for NaN trials, uniform emission (all zeros) so assignment is driven by transitions\\n   492→        log_emission = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\\n   493→        dist = np.maximum(zone_ranges[None, :, 0] - startpoints[valid, None],\\n   494→                          startpoints[valid, None] - zone_ranges[None, :, 1]) # negative if inside the zone, positive if outside\\n   495→        dist = np.maximum(dist, 0)\\n   496→        log_emission[valid] = -0.5 * (dist / sigma) ** 2\\n   497→\\n   498→        # viterbi forward pass\\n   499→        log_delta = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states))\\n   500→        psi = np.zeros((n_trials, n_states), dtype=int)\\n   501→        log_delta[0] = log_emission[0]  # uniform prior\\n   502→        for t in range(1, n_trials):\\n   503→            for k in range(n_states):\\n   504→                scores = log_delta[t - 1] + log_trans[:, k]\\n   505→                psi[t, k] = np.argmax(scores)\\n   506→                log_delta[t, k] = scores[psi[t, k]] + log_emission[t, k]\\n   507→\\n   508→        # backtrack\\n   509→        states = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=int)\\n   510→        states[-1] = np.argmax(log_delta[-1])\\n   511→        for t in range(n_trials - 2, -1, -1):\\n   512→            states[t] = psi[t + 1, states[t + 1]]\\n   513→\\n   514→        # convert state indices to zone names\\n   515→        zone_labels = np.array([zone_names[s] for s in states])\\n   516→\\n   517→        # distance from each trial's startpoint to its assigned zone range\\n   518→        assigned_lo = zone_ranges[states, 0]\\n   519→        assigned_hi = zone_ranges[states, 1]\\n   520→        zone_dist = np.maximum(np.maximum(assigned_lo - startpoints, startpoints - assigned_hi), 0)\\n   521→        zone_dist[~valid] = np.nan\\n   522→\\n   523→        results[mouse_id] = {'zone_labels': zone_labels, 'states': states, 'zone_dist': zone_dist}\\n   524→\\n   525→    return results\\n   526→    \\n   527→\\n   528→def main():\\n   529→\\n   530→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Convert Sosa et al. 2024 NWB data to pickle format.')\\n   531→ We performed tenfold cross-validation in which we trained the decoder on 90% of the data and tested it on a held-out 10%, eith\\r\\ner training and testing within the trials before the switch or training on one set (before) and testing on the other set (after). Figure 3a shows decoder perfor\\r\\nmance from a single cross-validation fold, considering all data from an example session. To quantify decoding accuracy compared to chance, we next downsampled t\\r\\nhe data to match occupancy at each RR position bin (bin size 2\\u03c0\\u2009/\\u200945, ~10\\u2009cm), either within trials before the switch or in the last 30 trials after the switch\\r\\n(thereby matching trial numbers before and after). We then repeated model training and testing with 100 shuffled datasets for each session and cell subpopulatio\\r\\nn. In each shuffle, the timeseries of each cell was independently circularly shifted by a uniform random amount up to the number of samples in the session minus\\r\\n one. In Fig. 3b, model performance is reported as a mean decode score over time samples and cross-validation folds compared to the mean of the shuffles for eac\\r\\nh session. To evaluate decoder performance across sessions, we z-scored the decoder score of each session to its shuffle and binned the z-score as a function of\\r\\n RR position, then averaged across animals (Fig. 3c).\\r\\n\\r\\n# Sequence detection and quantification\\r\\n\\r\\nFor analysis of behavioral timescale sequential firing of neural subpopulations, we used the unsmoothed, spatially binned dF/F in circular track coordinates (no\\r\\nt aligned to reward, although aligning to reward makes no difference for the circular sequence order). We sorted neurons by their peak firing positions from act\\r\\nivity averaged over the odd trials before the switch. This sort was cross-validated by plotting the trial-averaged activity of the even trials before the switch\\r\\n (for example, left-hand columns of Fig. 4a, normalized to the mean activity of each cell within a session), then applying this sort to the trials after the swi\\r\\ntch. The sequence positions before versus after were then taken as the peak firing positions of the trial-averaged \\u2018even-before\\u2019 trials and the trial-averaged \\u2018\\r\\nafter\\u2019 trials. Preservation of sequence order was quantified as the circular\\u2013circular correlation coefficient between the sequence positions before versus after\\r\\n. Although a P\\u2009value can be directly computed for this correlation coefficient, its significance was further validated by randomly permuting the cell identities\\r\\n of the neurons after the switch and re-computing the correlation coefficient 1,000 times to obtain a null distribution. The observed correlation coefficient, r\\r\\nho, was considered significant if it was outside 95% of the null distribution using a two-tailed test. The P value was calculated as:\\r\\n\\r\\nP=\\\\frac{{n}_{\\\\left|{{\\\\rm{coef}}_{\\\\rm{shuf}}}\\\\right|\\\\ge \\\\left|{{\\\\rm{coef}}_{\\\\rm{obs}}}\\\\right|}+1}{{N}_{\\\\rm{perm}}+1},\\r\\n\\r\\nwhere {n}_{\\\\left|{{\\\\rm{coef}}_{\\\\rm{shuf}}}\\\\right|\\\\ge \\\\left|{{\\\\rm{coef}}_{\\\\rm{obs}}}\\\\right|} is the number of shuffled coefficients with absolute values greater\\r\\nthan or equal to the absolute value of the observed coefficient, and {N}_{\\\\rm{perm}} is the total number of shuffles. P\\u2009<\\u20090.001 indicates that the observed rho\\r\\nexceeded all 1,000 shuffles.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor sequences followed across days, we again used the cross-validated sort from trials before the switch (or the first half of trials if reward did not move) on\\r\\n the reference day (the first day in each day pair) and applied this sort to trials after the switch (or second half) on both the reference day and all trials o\\r\\nn the target day (the second day in the pair). To measure drift between days, we computed the across-day circular\\u2013circular correlation coefficient between the s\\r\\nequence positions on reference day \\u2018after\\u2019 trials versus target day \\u2018before\\u2019 trials. A minimum of five followed cells in the sequence was required to compute a\\r\\ncorrelation coefficient.\\r\\n\\r\\nTo quantify the density of sequences, we divided the number of cells with peaks in each 2\\u03c0\\u2009/\\u200945 position bin by the total number of place cells for that animal.\\r\\n These density curves were smoothed only for visualization with a one-bin s.d. Gaussian and are shown as the mean across animals per each switch day (Fig. 4 and\\r\\n Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). We visualized the expected uniform distribution as the fraction of place cells in each animal\\u2019s sequence on a given switch day, d\\r\\nivided by the number of position bins, averaged across animals.\\r\\nroot@eccb0de73ee8:/app# grep -n 'def calc_dff\\\\|def compute_dff\\\\|def dff' code/src/reward_relative/preprocessing.py\\r\\n289:def dff(f,\\r\\nroot@eccb0de73ee8:/app# grep -n 'def ' code/src/reward_relative/preprocessing.py\\r\\n17:def create_sess(basedir, scandir, vrdir, animal, date, scene, session, scan_number,\\r\\n132:def append_session_data(sess, scaninfo=False, VR=False, suite2p=False, behavior=False,\\r\\n177:def vr_align_to_mock_2P(vr_dataframe, scan_info, run_ttl_check=False, n_planes=1):\\r\\n218:    def column_filter(columns): return [\\r\\n289:def dff(f,\\r\\nroot@eccb0de73ee8:/app#\\r\\n\"\n/logs/agent/episode-71/debug.json-352-        },\n/logs/agent/episode-71/debug.json-353-        {\n/logs/agent/episode-71/debug.json-354-            \"role\": \"assistant\",\n/logs/agent/episode-71/debug.json:355:            \"content\": \"\\n\\nNow I have enough information to understand the pipeline. Normalize by the fraction of non-NaN values\\\\n    ones = np.ones_like(a)\\\\n    ones[nan_mask] = 0\\\\n    norm = gaussian_filter1d(ones, sig, axis=axis)\\\\n    norm[norm == 0] = 1  # avoid division by zero\\\\n    result = smoothed / norm\\\\n    result[nan_mask] = np.nan\\\\n    return result\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef determine_reward_zone_label(rz_start_pos):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Determine reward zone label (A/B/C) from start position.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    if np.isnan(rz_start_pos):\\\\n        return None\\\\n    for label, (start, end) in REWARD_ZONES.items():\\\\n        if start - 20 < rz_start_pos < end + 20:  # Get the minimum position where rzone is active\\\\n            rz_start_pos = trial_pos[rz_active].min()\\\\n            rz_starts[t] = rz_start_pos\\\\n            rz_labels[t] = determine_reward_zone_label(rz_start_pos)\\\\n    \\\\n    return rz_starts, rz_labels\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef get_reward_zone_for_trial(rz_labels, trial_idx):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Get the reward zone label for a specific trial.\\\\n    For omission trials, infer from neighboring trials.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    if rz_labels[trial_idx] is not None:\\\\n        return rz_labels[trial_idx]\\\\n    \\\\n    # Search forward and backward for nearest non-None label\\\\n    for offset in range(1, len(rz_labels)):\\\\n        if trial_idx - offset >= 0 and rz_labels[trial_idx - offset] is not None:\\\\n            return rz_labels[trial_idx - offset]\\\\n        if trial_idx + offset < len(rz_labels) and rz_labels[trial_idx + offset] is not None:\\\\n            return rz_labels[trial_idx + offset]\\\\n    \\\\n    return 'A'  # fallback\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef compute_distance_to_reward_zone(position, rz_start):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Compute signed distance from current position to nearest point in reward zone.\\\\n    Reward zone spans [rz_start, rz_start + 50].\\\\n    Negative = before reward zone, positive = after.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    rz_end = rz_start + 50.0\\\\n    distance = np.zeros_like(position)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Before reward zone\\\\n    before_mask = position < rz_start\\\\n    distance[before_mask] = position[before_mask] - rz_start\\\\n    \\\\n    # In reward zone\\\\n    in_mask = (position >= rz_start) & (position <= rz_end)\\\\n    distance[in_mask] = 0.0\\\\n    \\\\n    # After reward zone\\\\n    after_mask = position > rz_end\\\\n    distance[after_mask] = position[after_mask] - rz_end\\\\n    \\\\n    return distance\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef discretize_distance(distance):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Discretize distance to reward zone into 7 bins.\\\\n    0: < -50 cm\\\\n    1: -50 to -10 cm\\\\n    2: -10 cm to < 0 cm\\\\n    3: 0 cm\\\\n    4: >0 cm to +10 cm\\\\n    5: +10 to +50 cm\\\\n    6: > +50 cm\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    bins = np.zeros(len(distance), dtype=np.int64)\\\\n    bins[distance < -50] = 0\\\\n    bins[(distance >= -50) & (distance < -10)] = 1\\\\n    bins[(distance >= -10) & (distance < 0)] = 2\\\\n    bins[distance == 0] = 3\\\\n    bins[(distance > 0) & (distance <= 10)] = 4\\\\n    bins[(distance > 10) & (distance <= 50)] = 5\\\\n    bins[distance > 50] = 6\\\\n    return bins\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef discretize_position(position, n_bins=5):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Discretize absolute position into n_bins equal-sized bins.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    bin_edges = np.linspace(0, TRACK_LENGTH, n_bins + 1)\\\\n    bins = np.digitize(position, bin_edges[1:])  # 0 to n_bins-1\\\\n    bins = np.clip(bins, 0, n_bins - 1)\\\\n    return bins\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef discretize_speed(speed):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Discretize speed into 5 bins.\\\\n    0: < 2 cm/s\\\\n    1: 2-10 cm/s\\\\n    2: 10-20 cm/s\\\\n    3: 20-40 cm/s\\\\n    4: > 40 cm/s\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    bins = np.zeros(len(speed), dtype=np.int64)\\\\n    bins[speed < 2] = 0\\\\n    bins[(speed >= 2) & (speed < 10)] = 1\\\\n    bins[(speed >= 10) & (speed < 20)] = 2\\\\n    bins[(speed >= 20) & (speed < 40)] = 3\\\\n    bins[speed >= 40] = 4\\\\n    return bins\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef process_licks(lick_data, trial_start_inds, teleport_inds):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Process lick data following reference code logic.\\\\n    1. Detect and remove lick sensor errors\\\\n    2. Clip to [0, 1] (binary)\\\\n    3. Smooth with Gaussian\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    licks = np.copy(lick_data).astype(np.float64)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Lick sensor error correction per trial\\\\n    for t in range(len(trial_start_inds)):\\\\n        t_start = trial_start_inds[t]\\\\n        t_end = teleport_inds[t]\\\\n        trial_licks = licks[t_start:t_end]\\\\n        \\\\n        # If >35% of samples have cumulative lick count > 2, set to NaN\\\\n        if len(trial_licks) > 0:\\\\n            frac_high = np.sum(trial_licks > 2) / len(trial_licks)\\\\n            if frac_high > LICK_ERROR_THRESHOLD:\\\\n                licks[t_start:t_end] = np.nan\\\\n    \\\\n    # Clip to [0, 1]\\\\n    licks[licks > 1] = 1\\\\n    \\\\n    return licks\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef process_session(nwb_path, show_processing=False, session_idx=0):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Process a single NWB file and return trial-level data.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    t0 = time.time()\\\\n    \\\\n    f = h5py.File(nwb_path, 'r')\\\\n    \\\\n    # Extract metadata\\\\n    subj_id = f['general']['subject']['subject_id'][()].decode()\\\\n    sess_id = f['general']['session_id'][()].decode()\\\\n    \\\\n    # Extract behavioral data\\\\n    beh = f['processing']['behavior']['BehavioralTimeSeries']\\\\n    position = beh['position']['data'][:]\\\\n    speed_data = beh['speed']['data'][:]\\\\n    lick_data = beh['lick']['data'][:]\\\\n    rzone = beh['reward_zone']['data'][:]\\\\n    env_data = beh['environment']['data'][:]\\\\n    trial_start_markers = beh['trial_start']['data'][:]\\\\n    teleport_markers = beh['teleport']['data'][:]\\\\n    scanning = beh['scanning']['data'][:]\\\\n    reward_timestamps = beh['Reward']['timestamps'][:]\\\\n    pos_timestamps = beh['position']['timestamps'][:]\\\\n    \\\\n    # Extract neural data\\\\n    deconv_data = f['processing']['ophys']['Deconvolved']['plane0']['data'][:]  # (n_timepoints, n_rois)\\\\n    iscell = f['processing']['ophys']['ImageSegmentation']['PlaneSegmentation']['iscell'][:]\\\\n    \\\\n    f.close()\\\\n    \\\\n    # Filter neurons by iscell\\\\n    cell_mask = iscell[:, 0] == 1\\\\n    neural_all = deconv_data[:, cell_mask].T  # (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\\\n    n_neurons = neural_all.shape[0]\\\\n    n_timepoints = neural_all.shape[1]\\\\n    \\\\n    # Get trial boundaries\\\\n    trial_start_inds = np.where(trial_start_markers > 0)[0]\\\\n    teleport_inds = np.where(teleport_markers > 0)[0]\\\\n    n_trials = len(trial_start_inds)\\\\n    \\\\n    if n_trials != len(teleport_inds):\\\\n        print(f\\\\\\\"  WARNING: trial_start ({n_trials}) != teleport ({len(teleport_inds)}) count\\\\\\\")\\\\n        n_trials = min(n_trials, len(teleport_inds))\\\\n        trial_start_inds = trial_start_inds[:n_trials]\\\\n        teleport_inds = teleport_inds[:n_trials]\\\\n    \\\\n    # Compute frame rate\\\\n    dt = np.median(np.diff(pos_timestamps))\\\\n    \\\\n    # Get reward zone info per trial\\\\n    rz_starts, rz_labels = get_reward_zone_start_per_trial(\\\\n        position, rzone, trial_start_inds, teleport_inds)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Process licks\\\\n    licks_processed = process_licks(lick_data, trial_start_inds, teleport_inds)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Determine reward per trial\\\\n    # Convert reward timestamps to frame indices\\\\n    reward_frame_inds = np.searchsorted(pos_timestamps, reward_timestamps)\\\\n    reward_frame_inds = np.clip(reward_frame_inds, 0, n_timepoints - 1)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Build per-trial reward binary\\\\n    trial_rewarded = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=np.int64)\\\\n    for t in range(n_trials):\\\\n        t_start = trial_start_inds[t]\\\\n        t_end = teleport_inds[t]\\\\n        # Check if any reward was delivered in this trial\\\\n        reward_in_trial = np.any(\\\\n            (reward_frame_inds >= t_start) & (reward_frame_inds < t_end)\\\\n        )\\\\n        trial_rewarded[t] = 1 if reward_in_trial else 0\\\\n    \\\\n    # Get environment type per trial\\\\n    trial_env = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=np.int64)\\\\n    for t in range(n_trials):\\\\n        t_start = trial_start_inds[t]\\\\n        t_end = teleport_inds[t]\\\\n        env_vals = env_data[t_start:t_end]\\\\n        env_vals = env_vals[env_vals >= 0]  # exclude -1\\\\n        if len(env_vals) > 0:\\\\n            trial_env[t] = int(np.median(env_vals))\\\\n    \\\\n    # Get reward zone label per trial (for output)\\\\n    trial_rz_label = np.zeros(n_trials, dtype=np.int64)\\\\n    rz_label_map = {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 2}\\\\n    for t in range(n_trials):\\\\n        label = get_reward_zone_for_trial(rz_labels, t)\\\\n        trial_rz_label[t] = rz_label_map.get(label, 0)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Get reward zone start position per trial (for distance computation)\\\\n    # For omission trials, use the same reward zone as neighboring trials\\\\n    trial_rz_start = np.zeros(n_trials)\\\\n    for t in range(n_trials):\\\\n        label = get_reward_zone_for_trial(rz_labels, t)\\\\n        trial_rz_start[t] = REWARD_ZONES[label][0]\\\\n    \\\\n    # Build trial data\\\\n    neural_trials = []\\\\n    input_trials = []\\\\n    output_trials = []\\\\n    \\\\n    for t in range(n_trials):\\\\n        t_start = trial_start_inds[t]\\\\n        t_end = teleport_inds[t]\\\\n        n_tp = t_end - t_start\\\\n        \\\\n        if n_tp < 2:\\\\n            continue\\\\n        \\\\n        # Neural data for this trial\\\\n        trial_neural = neural_all[:, t_start:t_end].astype(np.float32)\\\\n        \\\\n        # --- INPUTS ---\\\\n        # Time from start of trial (seconds)\\\\n        time_from_start = np.arange(n_tp) * dt\\\\n        \\\\n        # Environment type (binary, per trial)\\\\n        env_type = float(trial_env[t])\\\\n        \\\\n        # Trial number (continuous, per trial)\\\\n        trial_num = float(t)\\\\n        \\\\n        # Previous trial outcome (binary, per trial)\\\\n        if t == 0:\\\\n            prev_outcome = 0.0\\\\n        else:\\\\n            prev_outcome = float(trial_rewarded[t - 1])\\\\n        \\\\n        # Build input array\\\\n        # Time-varying: time_from_start (n_tp,)\\\\n        # Per-trial: env_type, trial_num, prev_outcome\\\\n        input_data = np.zeros((4, n_tp), dtype=np.float32)\\\\n        input_data[0, :] = time_from_start\\\\n        input_data[1, :] = env_type\\\\n        input_data[2, :] = trial_num\\\\n        input_data[3, :] = prev_outcome\\\\n        \\\\n        # --- OUTPUTS ---\\\\n        trial_pos = position[t_start:t_end]\\\\n        trial_speed = speed_data[t_start:t_end]\\\\n        trial_licks = licks_processed[t_start:t_end]\\\\n        \\\\n        # Distance to reward zone (time-varying, discretized)\\\\n        rz_start = trial_rz_start[t]\\\\n        distance = compute_distance_to_reward_zone(trial_pos, rz_start)\\\\n        dist_bins = discretize_distance(distance)\\\\n        \\\\n        # Absolute position (time-varying, discretized into 5 bins)\\\\n        pos_bins = discretize_position(trial_pos, n_bins=5)\\\\n        \\\\n        # Speed (time-varying, discretized)\\\\n        speed_bins = discretize_speed(np.abs(trial_speed))  # use absolute speed\\\\n        \\\\n        # Lick (time-varying, binary)\\\\n        lick_binary = np.zeros(n_tp, dtype=np.int64)\\\\n        if not np.all(np.isnan(trial_licks)):\\\\n            # Smooth licks\\\\n            smoothed_licks = nansmooth(trial_licks, LICK_SMOOTH_SIGMA)\\\\n            # Convert to binary: > 0.5 threshold after smoothing\\\\n            lick_binary = (smoothed_licks > 0.5).astype(np.int64)\\\\n            lick_binary[np.isnan(smoothed_licks)] = 0\\\\n        \\\\n        # Reward zone location (per-trial)\\\\n        rz_loc = trial_rz_label[t]\\\\n        \\\\n        # Reward outcome (per-trial)\\\\n        reward_out = trial_rewarded[t]\\\\n        \\\\n        # Build output array\\\\n        # Time-varying: dist_bins, pos_bins, speed_bins, lick_binary\\\\n        # Per-trial: rz_loc, reward_out\\\\n        output_data = np.zeros((6, n_tp), dtype=np.int64)\\\\n        output_data[0, :] = dist_bins\\\\n        output_data[1, :] = pos_bins\\\\n        output_data[2, :] = speed_bins\\\\n        output_data[3, :] = lick_binary\\\\n        output_data[4, :] = rz_loc\\\\n        output_data[5, :] = reward_out\\\\n        \\\\n        neural_trials.append(trial_neural)\\\\n        input_trials.append(input_data)\\\\n        output_trials.append(output_data)\\\\n    \\\\n    elapsed = time.time() - t0\\\\n    print(f\\\\\\\"  {subj_id} ses-{sess_id}: {n_neurons} neurons, {len(neural_trials)} trials, \\\\\\\"\\\\n          f\\\\\\\"{n_tp} timepoints (last trial), dt={dt*1000:.1f}ms, {elapsed:.1f}s\\\\\\\")\\\\n    \\\\n    if show_processing and session_idx < 2:\\\\n        plot_processing(subj_id, sess_id, position, speed_data, licks_processed,\\\\n                       trial_start_inds, teleport_inds, neural_all, \\\\n                       rz_starts, rz_labels, trial_rewarded, trial_env,\\\\n                       pos_timestamps, dt, neural_trials, input_trials, output_trials,\\\\n                       session_idx)\\\\n    \\\\n    return {\\\\n        'neural_trials': neural_trials,\\\\n        'input_trials': input_trials,\\\\n        'output_trials': output_trials,\\\\n        'subj_id': subj_id,\\\\n        'sess_id': sess_id,\\\\n        'n_neurons': n_neurons,\\\\n        'dt': dt,\\\\n    }\\\\n\\\\n\\\\ndef plot_processing(subj_id, sess_id, position, speed, licks,\\\\n                   trial_start_inds, teleport_inds, neural_all,\\\\n                   rz_starts, rz_labels, trial_rewarded, trial_env,\\\\n                   pos_timestamps, dt, neural_trials, input_trials, output_trials,\\\\n                   session_idx):\\\\n    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"Plot processing steps for visual verification.\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    import matplotlib\\\\n    matplotlib.use('Agg')\\\\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\\\\n    \\\\n    fig, axes = plt.subplots(6, 2,      ax.set_title('Distance to RZ (Trial 0)')\\\\n    \\\\n    # Plot 6: Position bins (first trial)\\\\n    ax = axes[2, 1]\\\\n    if len(output_trials) > 0:\\\\n        ax.plot(output_trials[0][1, main():\\\\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Convert NWB data to decoder format')\\\\n    parser.add_argument('output', help='Output pickle file path')\\\\n parser.add_argument('--show-processing', action='store_true', help='Show processing plots')\\\\n    args = parser.parse_args()\\\\n    \\\\n    if args.sample:\\\\n        args.full = False\\\\n    \\\\n    print(\\\\\\\"=\\\\\\\" * 60)\\\\n    print(\\\\\\\"NWB to Decoder Format Conversion\\\\\\\")\\\\n    print(\\\\\\\"=\\\\\\\" * 60)\\\\n    \\\\n    # Find all NWB files\\\\n    nwb_files = sorted(glob.glob('data/sub-*/sub-*_ses-*_behavior+ophys.nwb'))\\\\n    print(f\\\\\\\"Found {len(nwb_files)} NWB files\\\\\\\")\\\\n    \\\\n    if args.sample:\\\\n        # Select 2 sessions from \\\\n    # Process all sessions\\\\n    all_neural = []\\\\n    all_input = []\\\\n    all_output = []\\\\n    all_subj_ids = []\\\\n    all_sess_ids = []\\\\n    all_n_neurons = []\\\\n    all_dts = brain_region_idx = []\\\\n    for n_neurons in all_n_neurons:\\\\n        brain_region_idx.append(np.zeros(n_neurons, dtype=np.int64))  # all CA1\\\\n    \\\\n    # Compute median dt for metadata\\\\n
